name: Gene Editing and Potential Cures
blurb: CRISPR approaches aiming at a one time treatment.
title: Gene Editing and Potential Cures
answer: Gene editing aims to switch off the LPA gene in liver cells permanently with a single treatment. CRISPR Therapeutics' CTX320 has entered phase 1. It is the earliest and most uncertain approach, and permanent changes raise safety questions that will take years to answer.

reading.body:
Gene editing for Lp(a) is the earliest and most uncertain approach to lowering it, with one candidate in phase 1 and no proof yet that it prevents disease.

The approach switches off the LPA gene in liver cells so they stop making apolipoprotein(a). It is delivered as editing machinery packaged in lipid nanoparticles, and the edit is intended to last for the life of those cells. That permanence is the whole point, and it is also the reason safety is studied more carefully here than for a drug a patient can stop taking.

The supporting research is early and mostly preclinical. One 2024 paper reports lipid nanoparticle delivery of TALEN mRNA targeting LPA in transgenic mice, with gene disruption and reduced plasma Lp(a). A 2025 paper uses genome-scale CRISPR screening to study how cells take up Lp(a). The clinical evidence consists of a single development: CTX320 entered phase 1 in August 2026. People born with naturally very low Lp(a) appear healthy, which is encouraging but is not the same as showing that an edited gene lowers cardiovascular risk.

What this does not tell you is whether the treatment works. Phase 1 mainly asks about safety, and off-target edits and the impossibility of restoring Lp(a) once the gene is switched off will take years to characterize. The data covers one candidate and a set of related papers, not a pipeline, and it contains no efficacy results in humans.

sections.body: A one time cure is a real research goal but not a near term option; follow the early safety data.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Gene editing delivers editing machinery, typically packaged in lipid nanoparticles, to the liver, where it cuts the LPA gene so cells stop making apolipoprotein(a). Unlike RNA drugs, the change is intended to last for the life of the edited cells.

That permanence is the attraction and the risk. Long term safety, off target edits, and what happens when Lp(a) can no longer be restored all need careful study. People born with naturally very low Lp(a) appear healthy, which is encouraging, but a treatment must still prove both safety and benefit in trials.

developments.text: CRISPR/Cas9 based liver gene editing targeting the LPA gene, CTX320, has entered phase 1 studies.
